So that would be an example of where the total cost wasn't shown up front, but once they actually reach the cart and reach the checkout, it gives them a reason to abandon. Now, I don't think most people have to worry about this cuz most people are transparent on pricing up front, but if you're not like IM8, it's definitely something to be split testing and keeping an eye on. So, let's go to an example of a bad checkout and a good checkout. Uh, right away on the right is a onepage checkout rather than a multistep. Now, onepage versus multi-step, it's going to be something that you need to split test at the end of the day. Um, from our data, one page does convert a little bit better. Right up the top here, we also have a call out on the free shipping threshold. So, we're reinforcing again trying to get an upsell and we're objection handling the number one thing here, which is that if the extra costs are too high, well, if you just spend $12 more, you'd get free shipping. And there's all the fast pay option, shop pay, Apple Pay, Google Pay. Moving down, we then don't need to create an account here. By default, they're checking out as guest. Over here, they need to make an account. We've shortened the delivery address enormously by having essentials only. We don't have all these extra lines. Then down the bottom, we have free returns and free shipping over $75. So, we're reinforcing that they can save this $6 if they just get their cart value up. Actually, looks like we made a mistake here. These guys should be getting free shipping, but oh well. What I don't like, and this is something that you just have to weigh up, is for the sake of this, we took the tax amount out. Issue is people might misinterpret this as they are also getting stung with an extra $8. That's not the case. The tax was inclusive within the original pricing. We're just breaking this out for them to clearly. So, we're just reinforcing that we're not actually charging them extra and that that's included. However, I also understand just removing that or minimizing it or changing the language to be able to make it clearer that we're not charging them extra. This has been included within the actual price. Then on the right, obviously, we've made an extreme version here. Shipping's getting added, tax is getting added, handling fees are getting added. So, there's an extra $26 that suddenly gets layered in. This is going to tank conversion rates. This is the worst thing that you could do. Um, so many people won't convert because of this. So, what's leaking on the left? all of the extra costs, no total visible up front. So, if we go up to the landing page from before, the price that was there is not the price now. Guest checkout is default. Full cost is shown up front. Super lean form. We're getting as little amount of information as possible whilst also still being able to verify if it's a genuine transaction. We've got a onepage checkout. We've got free shipping progress tied to average order value. Returns are made very obvious and reinforced down the bottom here. We're not having some obscure privacy and returns policy that people can click out to. Instead, it's very clear that they're getting 30-day free returns. And then in this case, we're also sending an email at an SMS abandonment flow, whereas in the one on the left, they're not. Now, I want to run you through the math that anyone selling you on CRO services is never going to run you through. To trust a 10 to 20% conversion left, you need roughly a,000 conversions per variant. At a 2.5% conversion rate, that's about 40,000 sessions per variant. So, if you were to do just a simple AB split test, you would need to push 80,000 sessions through this split test. Most brands at seven figures can't produce that on a single product page in a month. So, when an agency goes and shows you a green AB test result after 2 weeks on a page doing a 100 conversions, it's not a win. It's just noise that they're trying to convince you there's a statistical confident outcome on. Now, it also gets a lot worse than this because most people run these tests by checking them every single day and they stop the moment it starts to look like a significant outcome, which substantially inflates your false positive rate. So that even tests that look valid often aren't because you stop the moment it told you what you wanted to hear. So people will run these tests and then they'll just cut them short because it looks like, oh, obviously this one's more positive, but you haven't actually let it run for one, two, three, four weeks or whatever time duration you need to hit statistical relevancy on the session volume. And there's really good examples of how this gets contaminated all the time. For example, anytime you send a Clavio campaign, uh it will cause an artificial spike in conversion rates and revenue. And if this isn't set up really meticulously and well and the Clavio traffic can't hit these landing pages in any way, and this is obviously very dependent on the test design, it will completely throw the entire test off and ruin it. And some people will just run abs tests using a software on the landing page which is just going to fork traffic between the two landers. And if you do that, you're going to fork traffic from your Clavio email which is just going to completely throw the numbers around. And so if you're doing these tests, you really need to do them on custom landing pages that are only driving cold traffic from Meta. Even when you do that, like these are still flawed if you have extended time to purchase because a certain percentage of customers will have a multi-click journey, which means that they won't buy on first click. It will take them a few clicks potentially across a few channels to actually convert. And we've looked at this pretty closely on a lot of big brands that we work with. It tends to be like about 1.5. And so on average it takes 1.5 clicks across a meta ad for a user to convert. Which means that about 50% of people are taking more than one click to actually follow through and make the conversion which means that they could have clicked here on the first ad and then they click here on the second ad. Now technically yes. Could you set up an ad set or campaign structure with an ABsplit test within meta to fork traffic as well? Yeah. And there's there's good ways to do tests and as long as your test design is pretty good, you can try your best to do uh strong absplit testing on landing pages, but there is so much that goes into it and there is so much volume of sessions required and you need to be able to ensure that there's not too much contamination that would impact the results and most of that is rarely considered. Statistical relevancy is rarely considered and so you end up just and CRO really ends up kind of just being star signs for ecom. Like it's just people are putting tests together, saying they're getting statistical outcomes, they're not getting statistical outcomes, and then they're just continuing to optimize all day long, and then you zoom out and look at a 2-year trend, and you're like, "Hey, revenue per session is the same. Revenue per visitor is the same. Conversion rates, for what they're worth, are the same." And so, what are we even doing here? Now, that's not to say that you shouldn't be AB split testing. That's not to say that conversion rate agencies are bad and you shouldn't use them. I think conversion rate agencies are actually good. And I think that we could probably put together an incredible conversion rate service that is ongoing tests on a monthly basis that would be very high leverage for 8 9 figure brands.
